sections.heading: What does a gout flare feel like?
sections.body:
Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in and around joints, and it causes sudden flares of severe pain and swelling. The affected joint becomes hot and very tender, and the big toes, ankles, knees and fingers are the usual places. Left untreated, an attack usually lasts about one to two weeks. If gout is not treated, future attacks may last even longer.

Almost everyone with gout has further flares, and these usually come within a year. Over time the attacks can become more frequent and longer, which may lead to chronic gout with lumps of uric acid crystals called tophi. The severe pain can make everyday tasks and getting around difficult.

sections.heading: How is gout diagnosed?
sections.body:
At an appointment, a GP will usually ask about your symptoms and medical history and examine the affected joint. They may also ask about your diet and whether anyone in your family has had gout. A blood test for uric acid may be done, but the level in the blood often falls during a flare. Because of this, a GP may wait about four weeks after a flare before doing the test.

A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out. When the diagnosis is uncertain, fluid can be taken from the joint and looked at under a microscope for crystals. An ultrasound or a special CT scan can also check for crystal build-up in the joint. If the picture is still unclear, a GP may refer you to a rheumatologist, a joint specialist, for further tests.

sections.heading: How is a gout flare treated?
sections.body:
Treatment has two parts: easing a flare, and preventing future flares. NICE recommends an anti-inflammatory painkiller (an NSAID) or a short course of steroid tablets as the first choice for a flare. A steroid injection is an option when those medicines and colchicine cannot be used. Colchicine is another option, and NIAMS notes that it works best when it is started as soon as symptoms appear.

NHS Inform advises starting medicine as early as possible, and it should begin to work within two or three days. Ice packs can also ease symptoms. For flares at night, Versus Arthritis suggests raising the joint on a cushion, using ice and keeping bedsheets off the sore area.

sections.heading: How are future flares prevented?
sections.body:
NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment, which aims to clear the urate crystals and prevent flares. NICE says this treatment can also shrink tophi and prevent long-term joint damage. NHS Inform says lifelong treatment is usually needed.

Flares can increase when urate-lowering medicine is first started, so doctors may give another medicine alongside it for the first months. NICE also notes that starting allopurinol gently and building up gradually causes fewer flares than a high start. NIAMS says lifestyle changes alone are not enough when flares are frequent or tophi are present, so medicine is the main approach. Diet changes can still help alongside medicine.

sections.heading: What diet and lifestyle changes help?
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It says small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk, and it suggests spreading any drinking across the week. It advises losing weight gradually, because crash diets can raise urate levels and losing too much weight too soon can trigger an attack. The NHS also advises avoiding crash diets and drinking plenty of fluids so that you do not get dehydrated.

Versus Arthritis suggests cutting down on sweetened soft drinks and says skimmed milk and low-fat yoghurt may help prevent attacks. The NHS and other sources also suggest limiting purine-rich foods such as red meat and seafood. The NHS says vitamin C supplements may help a little, but you should talk to a GP first because they are not suitable for everyone.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
Leaving gout untreated may cause lasting damage to the joints. Gout can also affect your mood, work and home life, and the pain can lead to feelings of depression or anxiety. NIAMS lists care for related conditions, such as heart and kidney disease, as part of treatment. NHS sources describe gout as manageable, because medicines can help the pain and healthier lifestyle choices can help prevent future attacks.

See a GP at a routine appointment if you have symptoms of gout for the first time, or if you have gout and your usual treatments are not helping. Get an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a swollen joint gets worse, or if you also have a high temperature of 38C or above, or feel sick or unable to eat. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis.

faqs.q: How long does a gout attack last?
faqs.a: Left untreated, a gout attack usually lasts about one to two weeks. Without treatment, later attacks may last even longer. Medicine taken as soon as possible should start to work within about two days, according to the NHS, so it helps to take it early.

faqs.q: Does gout go away on its own?
faqs.a: A single flare usually settles by itself, but almost everyone with gout has further flares, usually within a year. NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment to prevent flares. The NHS advises seeing a GP if you have gout and your usual treatments are not helping.

faqs.q: Should I have a uric acid blood test during a flare?
faqs.a: The level of urate in the blood often falls during a flare, so a test then can be misleading. A GP may wait about four weeks after a flare before doing it. A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out.

faqs.q: Is beer worse than wine for gout?
faqs.a: Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It treats beer as the worst option because of its purine content, and says small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk. Spreading any drinking across the week is also suggested.

faqs.q: When should I get urgent help for a swollen joint?
faqs.a: Get an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a swollen joint gets worse, or if you also have a high temperature or feel sick or unable to eat. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis. A first-time episode of gout symptoms should be seen by a GP.
